articles.title: "One card, one context" sat in the docs for two weeks. Then one day cost ~420M tokens, and the guard got bypassed the day after
articles.excerpt: The short version: a rule that limits how long an agent's context gets cannot live at the "entrance". It has to live inside the command the agent cannot avoid, and every action that moves work forward…
articles.body: The short version: a rule that limits how long an agent's context gets cannot live at the "entrance". It has to live inside the command the agent cannot avoid, and every action that moves work forward has to check it. I wrote "one task card, one fresh context" into my instructions and nothing enforced it for two weeks. The first time I turned it into code, it was bypassed within a day. Some background. I use Claude Code to split work into task cards and review the results, and Codex to implement them. Dispatching, monitoring and accepting a card is supposed to happen in a short context opened for that card alone. Failure one: the rule was only a sentence The rule dates from a review on October 30.

articles.title: Charge only when it is delivered: hold-then-capture balances in Laravel
articles.excerpt: If you sell something that may or may not be delivered, charging up front and refunding later works, but it is ugly. We run an SMS verification service, and a number that never receives its code used…
articles.body: If you sell something that may or may not be delivered, charging up front and refunding later works, but it is ugly. We run an SMS verification service, and a number that never receives its code used to leave two lines in the customer's history: a purchase and, minutes later, a refund. The money came back, but customers still saw "deductions" for things they never got and asked why they were charged. So we switched to authorize, then capture : buying a number only puts the price on hold, and the charge happens when the code arrives. This post shows the pattern in Laravel with a ledger-based wallet. It is small, but there are a few traps. The model Two numbers per user instead of one: balance : money the customer owns.

articles.title: At Ignite 2026, the agent race moved to context, control and price
articles.excerpt: Something shifted at this year's Microsoft Ignite, and it was not a model. On Tuesday, Microsoft used its Ignite stage, and partners timed their own releases to the same day, to announce enterprise ag…
articles.body: Something shifted at this year's Microsoft Ignite, and it was not a model. On Tuesday, Microsoft used its Ignite stage, and partners timed their own releases to the same day, to announce enterprise agent products. The pattern was consistent: the competition has moved from who has the smartest model to who grounds agents in your data, who governs what they may do, and how you pay for the work they complete. Start with context. Microsoft's headline platform announcement was Microsoft IQ, an "enterprise context management platform" that combines four context layers - Work IQ (documents, meetings and collaboration), Fabric IQ (governed business data), Foundry IQ (policies and institutional knowledge) and Web IQ - with more than 350 third-party connectors.

articles.body: Con pseudo-elementi e selettori intelligenti puoi segnalare subito markup incompleto, violazioni di layout e problemi di accessibilità. Nel lavoro quotidiano capita spesso di scrivere CSS pulito e robusto… e poi vedere i componenti usati in modo improprio. Il problema non è (solo) “chi sbaglia”: è che l’errore è facile da fare e difficile da notare, soprattutto in codebase grandi o con molti contributor. Un pattern sorprendentemente efficace è aggiungere messaggi d’errore direttamente in CSS : quando un componente non rispetta i requisiti minimi di markup o di accessibilità, lo evidenzi con un’outline e un testo esplicito. articles.title: The furnace clicks: what an AI voice agent needs to answer before the appointment
articles.excerpt: A homeowner calls a heating company just after 7 a.m.: "My furnace clicks every time it kicks on. Should I worry?" For a person at the front desk, that's an easy call if they know the customer and the…
articles.body: A homeowner calls a heating company just after 7 a.m.: "My furnace clicks every time it kicks on. Should I worry?" For a person at the front desk, that's an easy call if they know the customer and the equipment. For an AI voice agent, it's a good test of whether the agent is actually wired into the business or just reading a script. Here's what has to be in place for the answer to be right. 1. Knowing who's calling The agent has to match the caller ID to a customer record before it says anything useful. Without that, "on your model" is impossible, and every call starts with twenty questions. 2. An answer the business wrote, not one the model guessed "That's the igniter; on your model it usually means a dirty flame sensor" is technician knowledge.

articles.title: The SVG Badge Was Exactly 2 Units from Both Edges. Why Did the Test Fail?
articles.excerpt: We asked Codex to move a circular badge to the bottom-right corner of a folder icon using IconVectors over MCP. The icon had a 24 × 24 viewBox. The badge had to keep its diameter of 6 SVG units, leave…
articles.body: We asked Codex to move a circular badge to the bottom-right corner of a folder icon using IconVectors over MCP. The icon had a 24 × 24 viewBox. The badge had to keep its diameter of 6 SVG units, leave exactly 2 units of clearance on the right and bottom, and preserve the folder artwork. The first test returned FAIL . We opened the saved SVG in Chromium and measured both gaps independently. Right gap: 2 units . Bottom gap: 2 units . Where did the badge land? The badge started inside a group with transform="translate(2 1)" . That matters because the circle’s cx and cy describe its center inside the group. The requested gaps were measured from the edges of the whole icon. We could work out the expected position on paper. On each axis, the far edge of the badge should land at 24 − 2 = 22 .

articles.title: 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space
articles.excerpt: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft has officially hit one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026.
articles.body: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe. Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later.
